attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed open letter. It is one of his five operational predictions.

semantics.note: 'Will not' is firm language, so this is a scored forecast. The drafter kept the 'beyond the literal text' qualifier, the open-ended 'etc.' and the 2029 horizon.

contract.note: The plain reading (dependable comprehension of whole novels, including inference) is ordinary and fair. Letting an earlier capability that lasts into 2029 refute the forecast is a reasonable reading of 'In 2029'. Scoring this forecast apart from the wager matches the text.

evidence.note: PRELUDE (Aug 2025) finds models trailing humans by more than 15% on a related inference task. That is a pre-deadline failure, and failures before the deadline cannot settle the negative forecast.
Sept 2026 study of a small local model on detective novels with limited accuracy. It does not measure frontier systems and does not meet the early-resolution rule.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is 2029-12-31, after the evaluation date. No dated, independently assessed and reproducible demonstration of reliable whole-novel comprehension is in the packet, so the early contradiction rule is not met. Earlier failures cannot confirm the forecast. The forecast is not yet scoreable.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed open letter to Musk.

semantics.note: 'Hence' links the reliance on deep learning to the problems with unexpected situations, so causal fits. 'So far as I know' is a caveat about his knowledge, not a probability hedge.

contract.note: Reading 'hash-table-like' as a metaphor for reliance on learned patterns is a fair, ordinary reading. The result depends on how 'mostly' and 'a lot of problems' are defined, and the speaker defined neither.

evidence.note: Tesla's Aug 2021 disclosure that it uses neural networks for perception. It predates the target period and identifies no failure cause.
The same presentation describes explicit search and optimization in planning, which partly undercuts 'mostly lookup'. It does not show whether learned perception explains the failures.
NHTSA opened an investigation in Feb 2022 after 354 phantom-braking complaints. It reached no causal finding, and the braking was not necessarily triggered by unusual situations.

reviews.rationale: The contract asks for failure analyses that tie unusual-situation failures to reliance on learned patterns. The packet has architecture disclosures that point both ways and an open complaint investigation with no causal finding. Nothing establishes or refutes the causal link for 2022.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed open letter.

semantics.note: Firm historical observation covering four domains and roughly five years. The drafter's wording keeps 'anything like stable or trustworthy' and 'scarcely changed'.

contract.note: In the context of his pie chart, reading 'scarcely changed' as being about whether dependable general solutions exist, not benchmark scores, is fair. There is no reliability threshold, so interpretation drives the result.

evidence.note: 2017 adversarial study shows brittle reading comprehension at the baseline. It supports the starting state only.
2021 study finds language models struggle with abstract analogies and are sensitive to settings. This is partial support for the analogy domain.
Jan 2022 survey says commonsense reasoning tasks remain far from solved. This is partial support near the endpoint.
PaLM (Apr 2022) reports large benchmark gains. Under the contract these are not dependable general solutions, but they show substantial change in capability.

reviews.rationale: The evidence points to persistent reliability limits in language, analogy and commonsense, so the first clause looks partly supported. The support condition also needs comparable longitudinal evidence that broad reliability scarcely changed over 2017 to 2022, and the packet has none. PaLM's gains complicate the picture. The evidence does not settle the claim as a whole.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed open letter.

semantics.note: An open-ended necessity claim combined with an observation about proposals as of 2022. Both clauses are hedged with 'I don't think', a graded belief like 'I suspect'. The drafter's 'unlikely' modality reflects this.

contract.note: The contract admits that 'I don't think' expresses uncertainty but still sets it up for scoring on a plain reading. Policy applies plain readings only to firm language. 'Solving', 'good proposal' and 'AGI' are undefined, so the evaluator would supply the meaning.

evidence.note: MLTRL is a methodology proposal from before the post. Its own authors say it is not a cure-all, so it does not settle whether a 'good proposal' existed.
Secondary review (Sept 2026) finds no accepted AGI test and no established AGI. It offers no counterexample and no evidence on the antecedent.

reviews.rationale: Both clauses are framed as hedged belief ('I don't think'), which policy does not score. The forecast also has no deadline, and its antecedent (the methodology problem staying unsolved) is unknown. The packet has no verified AGI demonstration that would meet the early-resolution rule.
